analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to offer workers affordable family health coverage and help pay for it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the nation's basic wage-and-hours law to require any employer with 50 or more employees — counting contract workers — to offer every employee a family health plan as good as the standard Blue Cross plan federal workers get, and to pay the same share of the premium the federal government pays for its own workers. Employees would pay their share through payroll deduction. Workers on Medicare, Medicaid, or other federal health programs would generally have to take the employer offer. Employers that failed to comply would face federal civil penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 50 or more employees — including contract workers counted as employees — and their spouses and children. The bill's own findings note that most of the roughly 40 million uninsured Americans were workers or their dependents, so the people who stand to gain are working families who currently go without coverage or can't afford it. It also helps insurers and brokers selling employer plans, since every covered employer becomes a customer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at 50-plus-employee firms and their families

how_it_helps.text: Every employer with 50 or more employees would have to offer each worker a plan covering the worker and family with benefits at least as valuable as the FEHBP Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan as of 2002 [S2] [S3].

The employer would have to contribute at least the same share of the premium that the federal government contributes for its own employees under that plan, with prorated contributions for part-timers working 10 to 30 hours a week [S2] [S3].
Coverage would have to begin within 30 days of an employee's first hour of work, so new hires would not be left waiting months for insurance [S3].
Enforcement would come through ERISA civil money penalties and Fair Labor Standards Act injunctive relief, giving the government real tools against employers that refuse to comply [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers bear a new mandatory benefits cost — the federal-share portion of a family premium for every worker, including contract workers. Employees pay the remainder of the premium through mandatory payroll withholding. Because the bill requires workers on Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, or CHAMPUS to take the employer coverage, and lets federal programs be billed for the employee share of premiums (with Medicaid required to treat this as a state-plan obligation), some cost also shifts to public health programs. Staffing agencies and other intermediaries could absorb new costs under the contract-worker and single-client provisions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers, workers' paychecks, public programs

drawbacks.text: A blanket employer mandate raises labor costs for companies with 50 or more employees; businesses and economists commonly warn such mandates can slow hiring or reduce wages, and the bill applies to firms of that size with no small-business phase-in beyond the 50-employee threshold [S2] [S3].

Counting contract workers as the client company's employees, and covering any employer whose workers mainly serve one large client, would impose the mandate on staffing and contracting firms that did not directly set employment terms [S3].

The bill pushes workers on Medicare, Medicaid, and military-family coverage into employer plans and requires Medicaid, through state plans, to pay employees' premium shares — shifting costs onto public programs rather than reducing them [S3].
The benefit benchmark is frozen to a specific 2002 federal employee plan, so the required package would not automatically keep pace with medical practice over time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of uninsured working families the bill targets, guaranteed family coverage with a substantial employer contribution is a large, direct benefit, and the cost is one that employer-based insurance already imposes informally on covered firms. The honest objections are the mandate's effect on hiring and wages at mid-sized firms, the blurred line it draws for contract and staffing workers, and the fact that it funnels the expansion entirely through private employer plans rather than any broader public option — but as a working-family health coverage bill, the benefits are concrete and the costs are the standard trade-off any employer mandate carries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the Congress, referred to five committees, then sent to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on November 13, 2002 — just over a week after that year's elections, in the closing weeks of the 107th Congress [S1] [S5].

The Speaker referred it to five committees — Education and the Workforce (lead), plus Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services — a multi-committee referral that makes advance difficult because any one panel can hold a bill [S5].

On November 22, 2002, the Education and the Workforce Committee referred it to its Health Subcommittee; no further action of any kind appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired with the Congress [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers are better off because the bill died — they avoid a new federal requirement to pay a large share of family health premiums for all workers, including contract workers. Health insurers also lose the wave of new mandated customers it would have created. Uninsured working families, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers that avoid the coverage mandate

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 13, 2002 and was its only supporter in Congress; no colleague cosponsored it

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral, chaired by a Republican in the Republican-controlled House
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent the bill to its Health Subcommittee on November 22, 2002; held no markup and took no further action before the Congress ended

against.what_they_did: Controlled every committee the bill was referred to and never brought it to the floor in the final weeks of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and no Republican or additional Democrat ever signed on, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from the fact that a lone Democrat introduced it into a newly reelected Republican House majority that took no action.

industries.note: The mandate would turn every large employer into a required buyer of a qualifying plan, and the bill explicitly obligates insurers offering employer coverage to comply with its requirements — a large new pool of mandated customers. Their gain runs alongside workers' gain here, since the coverage requirement is the mechanism delivering the benefit.

They would owe a federally mandated share of family premiums for every employee, including contract workers. Their cost saving from the bill's defeat is the mirror image of the coverage working families would have received.

The bill counts contract workers as employees of the client employer and covers firms whose workers mainly serve one large client, potentially making intermediaries responsible for premiums on workers placed at big companies.

industries.industry: Federal health programs (Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, CHAMPUS)
industries.note: Enrollees would generally be shifted onto employer coverage, but the bill requires the federal programs to pay employees' premium shares on request and treats that as a Medicaid state-plan duty — reducing some program liabilities while adding new payment obligations.
